title: Lace Faroese shawl
subtitle: A fingering-weight Faroese shawl with an allover lace body in the wings.
excerpt: A Faroese-construction shawl in fingering-weight wool with a plain garter shoulder gusset and an allover vine lace pattern filling the wings below. The shoulder gusset is worked in garter first, then the wing sections open into lace. Wingspan approximately 160 cm, total depth approximately 80 cm. About 450 g of fingering yarn.
sourceNotes: The Faroese construction is documented in Anny Evermann, Die Norwegischen Muster in der Strickerei (1902). The vine lace pattern in the wings uses the Victorian vine-and-leaf structure from Weldon's Practical Knitter, 10th series (1895), §Lace Shawls. Combining the Faroese construction with an allover lace wing is a contemporary synthesis.

glossaryTerms.definition: A five-section shawl construction from the Faroe Islands with two wings, two shoulder gussets, and a centre back. Gusset decreases and wing increases create a curved shoulder fit.
A length of smooth waste yarn threaded through all live stitches at a given row, allowing safe rip-back to that row.

content.text: shawl in fingering wool. The shoulder gussets are plain garter; the wings carry an allover vine lace pattern. Wingspan approximately 160 cm, depth approximately 80 cm.

The gussets are worked in garter stitch for their full shaping depth (approximately 7 RS rows) to keep the shoulder fit clean. Once the gusset shaping is complete, the wing sections transition to vine lace, which runs from that point to the cast-off edge. Thread a
every 50 rows through the lace section. Budget about 450 g (about 1,800 m / 1,970 yards) of fingering wool.

content.text: 24 stitches and 40 rows to 10 cm over vine lace on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. The lace gauge is slightly more open than stockinette gauge, helping to extend the wingspan. The garter gusset section (approximately 7 RS rows) runs at stockinette gauge (48 rows per 10 cm); this difference is too small to affect the fit.

Cast on 81 stitches. Place 4 markers dividing the shawl into: left wing (6), left gusset (15), centre back (39), right gusset (15), right wing (6). Work the Faroese shaping (wing increases, gusset decreases) in garter stitch for approximately 7 RS rows until the gusset sections reach 1 stitch each.

After the gussets are complete, remove the gusset markers and merge the remaining centre-back and wing sections. Work vine lace across the full width on RS rows while continuing wing increases at each edge: RS lace row: k1, yo, vine lace repeat across, yo, k1. WS rows: k3, p to last 3 sts, k3.
Vine lace RS row (6 sts): k1, yo, k2, ssk, k1. Continue until wingspan reaches 160 cm.
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off after a plain WS row.

Lace pattern misaligned at the garter-to-lace transition: the stitch count at the transition was not a multiple of 6. Work 1 to 3 extra plain garter rows before switching to lace to reach the nearest multiple of 6 in the body stitches.

Shawl not staying on shoulders: the gusset section was too short. Return to the gusset section and check that the inner edge of each gusset was decreased for at least 5 RS rows before merging the sections.
Soak 20 minutes in cool water, press out in towels. Block the garter shoulder gussets in their natural curve; pin the lace wings aggressively to open the vine motifs.
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry.
Use a more complex OXO or feather-and-fan motif in the lace wings for a more traditionally Shetland-influenced Faroese shawl.
